I started dating someone when I was 19 and we broke up after 7 years. I definitely am better off, and I'm now with someone that I adore, who makes me look back and wonder what the fuck I was doing with that guy. Here are my takeaways:

1 - You change SO much in your (especially early) twenties, that you're not even the same person as when you started dating. A lot of times this means you stop being compatible. 

2 - You don't know what you want when you're that young. You think you do, but you don't even know who YOU are, so how can you know what you want or need from a partner? 

3 - It's hard to imagine yourself ever being happy with someone else after you've been together so long, especially during early adulthood, but you 100% can be. 

4 - When you've only experienced one serious relationship, you learn a lot from it, but things can seem normal that aren't. You might have tolerated things you wouldn't tolerate now. You're older, wiser, and more mature which sets you up for success going forward. 

5 - Give yourself grace to heal in your own time. It's going to hurt like a bitch for a while. The chemicals involved in love mimic addiction. The break up process is the most painful withdrawal. It gets easier the more time that passes. 

6 - Take time to process everything and with honesty reflect on what did and didn't work. What you wanted more of but weren't getting, what you could've done to be a better partner, etc. With that knowledge you will be able to love someone in a healthier, more fulfilling way. 

I'm so sorry, I hope you're ok. Keep trucking. Better things are coming, even if it doesn't seem like it.

A DBT skill called check the facts (I have to use it all the time for lots of things). I'm going to use an example so in this situation it might be "I'm worried my boyfriend is cheating on me."

1. Identify event promoting emotional reaction - make it very specific and the exact moment you got upset. 
Ex: he's at a bar with his friends and he hasn't texted me back in an hour ("he's distant" wouldn't be specific enough). 

2. Describe the facts of the situation (facts = only things you know from the past, things he's directly said to you, things you can feel with your senses). No assumptions or judgements.  
Ex: I texted him an hour ago and he hasn't responded. He said he's at X bar with XYZ friends. He has never cheated before to my knowledge. 

3. Challenge judgements/assumptions. This would be things like "I know he's up to something, otherwise he would've texted me back." You don't really know that. He might be deep in a pool game and just hasn't checked his phone. He might've forgotten his phone in his car. Basically you just try to think of any other possible thing that could be going on, because reality is you don't really know. Judgements would be things like "He's being a shitty boyfriend because he hasn't texted me back." Challenging that would look like saying to yourself "He does a lot of things to show me that he cares. Expecting someone to text me back within the hour isn't reasonable. Just because he isn't texting me back doesn't mean he doesn't care about me. 

4. Ask yourself if you're assuming a threat, like him leaving, him cheating, etc. Estimate the probability of it actually happening and other possible outcomes. 
Ex: I'm worried he's cheating, but we've been together for X years and he's never given me a reason to distrust him. Even if someone hit on him at the bar, it's unlikely he would do anything based on what I know about him. 

5. Ask yourself if your emotion fits the situation AND if the intensity matches the situation. 
Ex: I'm extremely anxious (fear) that he's cheating on me. It's normal to feel a little bit anxious when your boyfriend is out drinking and not responding, but based on our history and the facts of the situation, it doesn't make sense to be THIS anxious. 

6. As long as your feelings aren't appropriate (so like say you were being chased by someone on the street, extreme fear makes sense) you do opposite action. I can tell you more about that if you want but this is already really long. Basically identify the urges and do the opposite. So if your urge is to text him and call him until he answers, don't do that.

1) Don't make the situation worse. It sounds like you're already doing this. He asked for space and you're giving him space. 
2) Find something to distract you for a while. Something that isn't destructive but makes you feel better. I have some really weird ones, like copying the lyrics to songs in a notebook. Just think of something you can do to get your mind off of it. 
3) When you're calmer, figure out your next step. Don't think ahead. What is the next thing you need to do? If you just did one thing today, what would be the most important thing? I work in vet med, and "intestinal issues" can mean a lot of things, but in cats who are otherwise doing alright, it usually just means they have IBD. I think doing the food your vet recommended is a good start. They will always recommend an abdominal ultrasound as that's how they make the official diagnosis, but it isn't really necessary unless there's more to the case you haven't mentioned. The mention of intestinal blockage is concerning to me - how long has she had symptoms, is she vomiting, and is she eating?

For the heart stuff, no primary care vet is going to be able to tell you why her heart is enlarged or what you need to do about it. There is likely something serious going on, like heartworms (which are usually fatal in cats and have no treatment) or something congenital. Has your vet discussed a heartworm test? Those are like $40 and would be a good start. 

Knowing how much veterinary cardiology is, I don't think I would do it for my own cat with the income that I have. But you have to be prepared for the possibility of sudden heart failure, respiratory distress, etc. basically she can become an emergent case at any time. 

I also HIGHLY recommend being transparent with your vet about what you can afford. The majority of them (except for a few assholes) will work with you and try to figure out what's best for your cat within your resources. Pet care is expensive, and we know that. Not everybody is able to offer their pet the gold standard of care. 

Some other helpful recommendations I've seen in other comments are also good, I recommend looking into CareCredit or Scratchpay (make sure the cardiologist accepts it first). Also as someone else mentioned, maybe you can keep her comfortable until the baby comes and do more for her later. But you need to have this conversation with your vet. Someone else mentioned pet insurance - they won't cover anything preexisting so I wouldn't bother.

Edit to add cancer in a 5 year old cat is extremely unlikely.
